Learning outcomes

By the end of today’s lecture, you will learn:

  • How to construct verifiable secret sharing, and how it can be used as the basis for MPC
  • How to construct Shamir secret sharing with any threshold for reconstruction

Review from last lecture

Unit 4 of the course is about protecting data science. My goal is to convince you that it is possible to conduct data science without data sharing.

A \((t, n)\)-secret sharing protocol:

  • splits a secret into \(n\) shares, such that any \(t + 1\) shares allow complete reconstruction of the secret
  • satisfies \(t\)-perfect secrecy, which says that the shares held by a coalition of \(\leq t\) parties reveal no information about the secret

We constructed two ways to split a secret \(s\) that are perfectly secret against a passive eavesdropper Eve who sees \(t = n - 1\) shares. The last share serves as a ‘one-time pad’ to protect the secret \(s\).

  • Boolean secret sharing: \(s = s_1 \oplus s_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus s_n\)
  • Arithmetic secret sharing: \(s = s_1 + s_2 + \cdots + s_n \bmod{2^\ell}\)

Cryptographically secure multi-party computation (MPC) allows parties to:

  • Work together to calculate \(y = f(\vec{x})\)
  • Ensure that no coalition of \(\leq t\) computing parties can learn anything about the input data

Last time, we constructed several MPC protocols:

  • Secure linear algebra with \(n = 2\) parties that tolerates \(t = 1\) passive eavesdropper Eve
  • Secure computation with \(n = 3\) parties that tolerates \(t = 1\) passive eavesdropper Eve
  • Secure computation with \(n = 4\) parties that tolerates \(t = 1\) actively malicious Mallory

20.1 Verifiable secret sharing

In today’s lecture, I want to discuss an alternative – and more foundational – way to build MPC that is secure against an actively-malicious adversary Mallory.

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \text{passively secure SS} & \longrightarrow & \text{passively secure MPC} \\ \downarrow & & \downarrow \\ \text{actively secure SS} & \longrightarrow & \text{actively secure MPC} \end{eqnarray*}\]

Recall how arithmetic secret sharing works. Suppose that Alice has secret data \(x\) and converts it into a collection of \(n\) secret shares:

\[ x = x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \bmod{2^\ell}\]

For now, suppose that Alice doesn’t even want to compute over this data; she just wants to outsource the data to several cloud providers and reconstruct it at some later date.

  • Alice can disperse the message among the cloud providers by giving share \(x_i\) to provider \(i\)

  • Many months or years later, Alice can retrieve the secret data by fetching all shares and adding them together

This provides excellent confidentiality: the cloud providers can perform their job of holding onto Alice’s data for a long time, but no coalition of \(n-1\) or fewer of them can ever learn the data.

However, if one party provides an incorrect share \(x_i^* = x_i + \Delta\), then Alice’s secret is going to be incorrect by \(\Delta\):

\[x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + (x_i + \Delta) + \cdots + x_n = x + \Delta \bmod{2^\ell}\]

This is bad news…

  • For Alice, because her data is corrupted and there’s no way for her to pinpoint which cloud provider is to blame
  • For the honest cloud providers, because Alice might refuse to pay them as a result of the data corruption, even though they properly did their job and held onto their share \(x_i\) for a long time

The problem

In other words, this problem looks similar to the Byzantine generals question. Alice is a leader and is providing information to many other parties.

The main differences here are that:

  • We are adding confidentiality through secret sharing, and
  • There are two stages to the protocol: a dispersal stage and a retrieval stage

But the other trust questions from the Byzantine generals problem remain. Alice does not necessarily trust the other parties entirely, and they don’t entirely trust Alice either.

Question. How can we provide each party with an integrity guarantee? That is:

  • During dispersal, the cloud providers want to be convinced that they’re holding onto a share of a real secret that Alice will pay them for
  • During retrieval, Alice wants to be convinced that the shares are correct, or be able to pinpoint which provider(s) are sending her bad shares

In fact, today’s approach will provide data confidentiality, integrity, and availability (i.e., all computing parties have shares of the data, and they know that everyone else has shares too).

A construction

One way to solve this problem is to use Merkle trees. Recall that Merkle trees allow for uploading many files to the cloud, so that the cloud can prove that each file is part of the overall collection.

Concretely, here is a protocol that everyone can follow to disperse the shares and later retrieve the message.

In dispersal:

  • Alice creates secret shares such that \(x = \sum x_i\), and builds a Merkle tree of all shares \(x_i\) (let’s call the Merkle root \(h\))
  • Alice sends each cloud provider its share \(x_i\), the Merkle root \(h\), and a Merkle proof \(\pi_i\)
  • The provider checks proof \(\pi_i\) to verify that the provided share \(x_i\) is consistent with the Merkle root \(h\)
  • Alice saves the (small) Merkle root \(h\) and deletes everything else

In retrieval:

  • Each cloud provider sends their share \(x_i\) and proof \(\pi_i\) to the leader
  • Alice verifies each proof, and pays the corresponding provider if it’s correct
  • If a provider has cheated, Alice detects the error and takes appropriate action (e.g., sue the cloud provider in court, or take money that the provider has placed in escrow in a smart contract, etc)

Interactive question. There is actually a bug in this protocol. What is it?

  1. A malicious cloud provider could not save its share after dispersal is complete, and honest leader Alice cannot detect this
  2. A malicious cloud provider could send an incorrect share \(x_i\) during retrieval, and honest leader Alice cannot detect this
  3. A malicious leader Alice could send shares that are inconsistent with the Merkle root \(h\), and honest providers cannot detect this
  4. A malicious leader Alice could send different Merkle roots \(h\) to each provider, and honest providers cannot detect this

Answer. Actually, all of these responses indicate issues we will need to tackle today.

  • Attacks A and B by a malicious cloud provider are detectable by Alice thanks to the Merkle proof, but currently Alice has no recourse against this attack since all shares are required to reconstruct the secret (we will address this issue later today)
  • Attack C is detectable by an honest provider, but the above pseudocode doesn’t say what the provider should do in response
  • Attack D is not detectable: if malicious Alice sends an incorrect Merkle tree root \(h^*\), then an honest cloud provider might verify that its share \(x_i\) is consistent with the wrong root and later be accused of cheating during the retrieval phase

We can fix this problem using techniques from earlier parts of this course! To reach agreement on the Merkle root \(h\), we can have the leader post the Merkle root \(h\) to a blockchain or run Byzantine Broadcast to disperse \(h\) to all providers.

Adding broadcast

In dispersal:

  • Alice creates secret shares such that \(x = \sum x_i\), and builds a Merkle tree of all shares \(x_i\) (let’s call the Merkle root \(h\))
  • Alice and providers conduct a Byzantine Broadcast to disperse the Merkle root \(h\) to all parties
  • Alice sends each cloud provider its share \(x_i\), the Merkle root \(h\), and a Merkle proof \(\pi_i\)
  • The provider checks proof \(\pi_i\) to verify that the provided share \(x_i\) is consistent with the Merkle root \(h\) and the provider refuses to participate further if this proof is incorrect
  • Alice saves the (small) Merkle root \(h\) and deletes everything else

The retrieval stage can work the same as before. And in fact, the leader doesn’t even need to store the Merkle root \(h\) because it can just request it from all providers later: if there is an honest majority or a PKI, then the leader can distinguish the correct \(h\) from an incorrect one sent by a faulty cloud provider.

20.2 From verifiable secret sharing to secure addition

So far, this technique works to disperse secret data and then retrieve it later.

Let’s bring back the idea of computing over secrets.

  • Suppose the leader Alice dispersed two secrets \(x\) and \(y\) using this protocol… or maybe two different leaders dispersed two different secrets, such as their company’s payroll data

  • Now, we only want to retrieve the overall sum \(x + y\) of the two secrets, rather than retrieving \(x\) and \(y\) individually

  • As we saw last time: if we can take the sum of two secrets, then it is straightforward to extend the idea in order to perform any linear algebra operation over several secrets

Can we do this? Well… not quite.

  • The good news is that the secret sharing protocol is linear, so the providers can just send shares \(x_i + y_i\) rather than separately sending each of the two summands
  • The bad news is that the Merkle tree is not linear, so provider \(i\) cannot prove that it is sending the right value \(x_i + y_i\)

So let’s replace the Merkle tree with something else.

Using the discrete log problem, we can create a new way to commit and prove properties of the secrets that is amenable to computation.

20.3 Commitments from discrete log

A Merkle tree is a special case of a kind of cryptographic primitive that we discussed at the beginning of the semester: a message commitment. Recall that commitments are a digital analog to putting a written message inside of an envelope and placing it on the table.

  • After Alice commits to a message, then everyone knows that the message is inside of the envelope, but
  • Nobody can read the message until the envelope is opened. (This is related to, but not the same thing as, encryption of a message.)

Commitments have two security requirements.

  • Binding: even against a malicious committer, it is infeasible for the committer to show a different message \(m^*\) in the open step than the message \(m\) that it originally used during the commit routine.
    Mallory Bob
    \(\quad \overset{c}{\longrightarrow} \quad\)
  • Hiding: even against a malicious receiver, from only the commitment \(c\) it is infeasible to learn anything about the message \(m\).
    Alice Mallory
    \(\overset{c}{\longrightarrow}\)

Feldman commitments

Let’s construct a commitment protocol. As is the norm in this course by now, we will construct commitments based on the hardness of some math problem, so that they are easy to compute but hard to invert.

Specifically, we will use the hardness of the discrete log problem. Remember that this problem states that for a uniformly random choice of \(x\):

  • \((g, x) \mapsto h = g^x\) is easy to compute, but
  • \((g, h) \mapsto x = \log_g(h)\) is hard to compute

Question. How can we construct a commitment protocol from discrete logs?

For today, we will only consider a simplified version of the problem where message \(m\) to be committed is itself chosen uniformly at random.

  • This isn’t usually the case: for instance, the messages that you send to your friends over the Internet probably have a lot of structure to them
  • But this will be the case for cryptographic secret shares, and that will suffice for us today

Here is a commitment protocol designed by Paul Feldman in 1987. As a starting point, assume that all parties agree upon some base element \(g\) (e.g., it is specified in some open standard).

  • commit(m): create the commitment \(c = g^m\)
  • open(c, m): reveal \(m\), so that the receiver can calculate \(g^m\) itself and check that it is equal to \(c\)

This commitment protocol achieves:

  • Binding because there is a one-to-one mapping between messages \(m\) and commitments \(c\), so it is impossible to open to any other message
  • Hiding because inverting \(c\) to recover \(m\) is computationally infeasible when \(m\) is chosen uniformly at random, according to the discrete log assumption

Additive homomorphism

We can use commitments to resolve the conundrum from before! As a reminder: we wanted to find a way to disperse several secrets, say \(x\) and \(y\), and then provide the option for the cloud providers to retrieve only the sum \(x + y\).

Specifically, we will use Feldman commitments to construct a new verifiable secret sharing protocol. The key insights here are that:

  • Each secret share individually is chosen uniformly at random, so we can use them in Feldman commitments
  • Feldman commitments are linear… well, sorta. Specifically, given the commitments to two messages \(g^{m_1}\) and \(g^{m_2}\), we can compute the commitment to their sum \(g^{m_1} \times g^{m_2} = g^{m_1 + m_2}\)

Technically, this isn’t linearity in the sense of a linear algebra course like DS 121, because we need to multiply the commitments in order to add the underlying messages.

So let’s give this property a fancy new name: additive homomorphism. We say that Feldman and Pedersen commitments are additively homomorphic, because given several commitments it is possible (somehow) to compute the commitment to the sum of the underlying messages.

20.4 VSS with commitments

Here is a new verifiable secret sharing protocol that we can use to disperse a secret over \(n\) cloud providers. As a starting point, we assume that there are \(n\) public constants \(g_1, g_2, \ldots, g_n\) that everybody knows before the protocol starts; importantly, they have nothing to do with our secrets.

In dispersal:

  • The leader creates all secret shares such that \(x = \sum x_i\), and calculates a commitment \(c_i = {g_i}^{x_i}\) to each share. Let’s call the vector of commitments \(\vec{c} = [c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n]\).
  • The leader and providers conduct a Byzantine Broadcast to disperse all commitments \(\vec{c}\). (That is, every provider agrees on the commitment for everyone, not just themselves.)
  • Then, the leader sends each cloud provider its share \(x_i\). The provider can check for itself that \({g_i}^{x_i}\) equals the public commitment \(c_i\), and refuses to participate further if the value is incorrect.
  • The leader saves the commitment vector \(\vec{c}\) and deletes everything else.

Retrieving \(x\) works similarly as before:

  • Each cloud provider sends their share \(x_i\).
  • The leader can check that \({g_i}^{x_i}\) equals the appropriate commitment inside the vector.

Secure computing with VSS

Now, let’s return to the problem of secure addition of secrets. Suppose that two secrets \(x\) and \(y\) have been dispersed to the same set of cloud providers, with corresponding commitment vectors \(\vec{c}_x = [g_i^{x_i} : i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}]\) and \(\vec{c}_y = [g_i^{y_i}: i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}]\).

The cloud providers can form a verifiable secret sharing of their sum \(z = x + y\) by:

  • Adding their individual shares \(z_i = x_i + y_i\).
  • Componentwise-multiplying \(\vec{c}_x\) and \(\vec{c}_y\) to form a new vector of commitments \(\vec{c}_z = [g_i^{x_i} g_i^{y_i} : i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}]\).

Why does this work?

  • The new commitment corresponding to \(z_i\) equals \(g_i^{x_i} \times g_i^{y_i} = g_i^{x_i + y_i}\), which is a valid Feldman commitment that will properly open and verify during the retrieval stage
  • So: we can retrieve \(z\) without ever learning the summands \(x\) and \(y\) individually!

Secure multiplication of secrets is more complicated so I will not show it today, but it is possible to construct. From this, we can do verifiably secure computation of any data analysis!

Vector commitments

One small downside of our construction is that we have to disperse a vector of commitments \(\vec{c}\).

  • The length of this vector equals the number of cloud providers \(n\), independent of the data size.
  • This is somewhat strange: if we increase the number of cloud providers to make the dispersal more secure, then we have to pay for this in extra storage size that is linear in \(n\).

By comparison, the Merkle tree looks nicer: the root \(h\) is independent of \(n\), and each individual proof \(\pi_i\) has size \(\log(n)\).

The good news is that it is possible to combine all of the commitments into a single element that has constant size, independent of both the message length and the number of providers!

  • The idea is simple and again is based on the hardness of discrete logarithms.

  • Rather than computing \(\vec{c} = [g_1^{x_1}, g_2^{x_2}, \ldots, g_n^{x_n}]\), we will instead compute a single commitment:

    \[\vec{c} = g_1^{x_1} \times g_2^{x_2} \times \cdots \times g_n^{x_n}.\]

This is called a vector commitment. The math of how to open such a commitment is not too difficult but beyond the scope of this course; it uses something called “bilinear maps.”

20.5 Threshold secret sharing

Today, we have built protocols based on verifiable secret sharing that allow a collection of parties to perform data science with confidentiality, integrity, and availability. To do so, we composed two protocols with different thresholds:

  • Verifiable secret sharing, which provides confidentiality and integrity (today we used arithmetic secret sharing, which has perfect secrecy against any coalition of \(t_c = n - 1\) adversarial parties)
  • Byzantine Broadcast, which provides availability

Without a PKI, we know that \(t_a < n/3\) is the best we can hope for in order to achieve data availability. But the confidentiality threshold \(t_c\) can be higher than this.

  • That is, we can protect the confidentiality of the data even in circumstances where the attacker controls enough parties that agreement breaks and we can no longer guarantee correct retrieval of the data

  • This is a subtle point, and the research papers on verifiable secret sharing missed it for decades!

Definition 1 (Dual-threshold VSS) A dual-threshold verifiable secret sharing protocol supports \(t_c > t_a\). The highest privacy threshold possible is \(t_c = n - 1\).

Fault tolerance

Should we always choose the highest confidentiality threshold \(t_c = n - 1\)? Not necessarily. Because up to \(t_c\) parties cannot recover the data, there is an inherent tradeoff between confidentiality and fault tolerance of accidental mistakes.

We are writing in connection with the recent IACR 2025 election conducted using the Helios electronic voting system. … Three members of the IACR 2025 Election Committee acted as independent trustees, each holding a portion of the cryptographic key material required to jointly decrypt the results. This aspect of Helios’ design ensures that no two trustees could collude to determine the outcome of an election or the contents of individual votes on their own: all trustees must provide their decryption shares.

Unfortunately, one of the three trustees has irretrievably lost their private key, an honest but unfortunate human mistake, and therefore cannot compute their decryption share. As a result, Helios is unable to complete the decryption process, and it is technically impossible for us to obtain or verify the final outcome of this election. … After careful consideration, we have decided that the only responsible course of action is to void this election and start a new election from scratch.

– Statement by the IACR 2025 election committee in November 2025 (emphasis mine)

Shamir secret sharing

There is a more flexible way to design secret sharing to allow for any confidentiality threshold \(t_c\). It was discovered by Adi Shamir in 1979, and it is named Shamir secret sharing in his honor.

This secret sharing protocol uses polynomials to encode a secret. First, a quick math refresher.

Interactive question. How many points in space are required to uniquely determine a line?

  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4

This idea generalizes to higher-degree polynomials:

  • Any 2 points uniquely define a line (i.e., a polynomial of degree 1)
  • Any 3 points uniquely define a parabola (i.e., a polynomial of degree 2)
  • Any 4 points uniquely define a cubic (i.e., a polynomial of degree 3)
  • Any 5 points uniquely define a quartic (i.e., a polynomial of degree 4)
  • …and so on

Shamir secret sharing uses this idea to encode a secret \(s\) with any confidentiality threshold \(t_c\).

  • split \(s\) by randomly choosing a polynomial \(p\) of degree \(t_c\) with \(p(0) = s\), and then form the shares \(s_1 = p(1)\), \(s_2 = p(2)\), …
  • reconstruct a secret from any \(t_c + 1\) shares using polynomial interpolation to compute \(p\), and then output the secret \(s = p(0)\)

Example. In order to split a secret among 5 parties such that any 3 of the 5 people can reconstruct the secret, randomly sample a polynomial of degree \(t_c = 2\) whose \(y\)-intercept is the secret.

import numpy as np

s = 0                            # the secret
xvals = np.linspace(-1, 6)       # define x values
yvals = []                       # define y values
for x in xvals:
  yvals.append(s + 4 * x - x**2) # polynomial with secret at the y-intercept

Asynchrony

In today’s lecture, I have discussed protocols that have clearly-defined rounds – that is, I’ve assumed that the network is synchronous. It is important that the cloud providers receive their shares after a short delay, so that they can complain instantly and publicly if they have not received shares that are consistent with the commitment.

One could ask the same question in the asynchronous setting. That is, we could ask for asynchronous verifiable secret sharing. Constructing this primitive is more subtle than what we did today, for several reasons:

  • The best possible confidentiality threshold is now \(t_c = n - t_a\), since some parties might never show up to reconstruction and it is impossible to determine whether they are slow or evading you
  • The dispersal phase cannot include a step where a provider complains if their shares are inconsistent with the commitment, because asynchronous protocols are slow and the provider might not get its information for a long time
  • Termination is no longer guaranteed, as with all asynchronous protocols

To my knowledge, the fastest asynchronous verifiable secret sharing protocol is one that BU postdoc Nicolas Alhaddad, former BU undergrad Ziling Yang, and I built last year.

  • It is based on Shamir secret sharing
  • It is dual-threshold
  • It is a building block toward the construction of MPC in the asynchronous setting

If you’re interested, here is the research paper with all of the details: https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/326.pdf.
